tasks.task_description: Part (a): build a model of passenger flow through a US airport security checkpoint, identify where the bottlenecks are in the current process, and locate the problem areas. Scope: the four-zone process (Zone A ID check, Zone B divestiture + X-ray belt + body scanner, Zone C collection, Zone D secondary search), with separate TSA Pre-Check and regular lanes at the 1:3 lane ratio stated in the problem.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a discrete-event simulation (DES) of the checkpoint as a pipeline of serial resources, implemented in code/checkpoint_sim.py. Each lane is modeled as four serial stages — ID officer (10 s), divest/bin staging (45 s regular, 18 s Pre-Check, sharing a capacity-limited staging area), X-ray belt (30 s per bin batch), body scanner (20 s, in parallel with the belt) — followed by a shared collection belt (12 s) and a shared Zone-D pool of secondary-search officers (150 s each) that flagged passengers join. Passengers arrive as Poisson streams (95/hour base = 40 Pre-Check + 55 regular, matching the 45% Pre-Check share in the problem statement; 140/hour peak scenario), and time-pressed travelers can abandon after 12 minutes (a few percent, per expert exchange 10). Why DES is sound here: the checkpoint is a network of heterogeneous, partially parallel, serial resources with stochastic service times and a feedback loop (secondaries), so closed-form queueing theory (M/M/c) would misrepresent it; DES preserves the actual process topology and lets each stage's queue length be read directly as a bottleneck diagnostic. Assumptions: single checkpoint with 2 Pre-Check + 6 regular lanes; officers do not idle (they pre-stage work, per expert exchange 6); no mid-queue line switching (expert exchange 5: staying put is the dominant behavior); the dataset's sparse officer columns are treated as service-time samples, not as paired passenger records.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: DES event loop. State per lane i: id_free[i], belt_free[i], body_free[i]; global: staging_free, collect_free, sec_free[o] for o = 1..S secondary officers. For a passenger arriving at time t on lane i: (1) ID: start = max(t, id_free[i]), id_end = start + 10; (2) divest/staging: st_start = max(id_end, staging_free), bin_ready = st_start + D, where D = 45*c*(0.4 if Pre-Check else 1) seconds and c is the culture multiplier in {0.85, 1.0, 1.25}; (3) body scan: body_end = max(bin_ready, body_free[i]) + 20; (4) belt: belt_end = max(bin_ready, belt_free[i]) + 30; (5) collection: col_end = max(belt_end, body_end, collect_free) + 12; (6) secondary: with probability p = 0.05 (Pre-Check) or 0.14 (regular) the passenger joins the free secondary officer: done = max(col_end, sec_free[o]) + 150*c; otherwise done = col_end. Throughput and wait are measured per passenger as done - t. Bottleneck diagnostic: the stage whose resource's busy time is closest to 100% of the horizon and whose queue length is largest. Parameter table (empirical inputs; every value is from the task dataset or an exchange, none from memory): ID time = 10 s, interval [5.3, 15.4], source: dataset column 'ID Check Process Time 1' (n=9, mean 10.2 s); divest time = 45 s, interval [35, 60], source: expert exchange 6 (pre-staging context), Pre-Check fraction 0.4 from the problem statement's exemption list; belt batch = 30 s, interval [5, 68], source: dataset 'Time to get scanned property' (n=29, mean 28.6 s); body scanner = 20 s, interval [10, 60], source: expert exchange 2; collection = 12 s, interval [8, 20], source: expert exchange 2; secondary rate p = 0.14, interval [0.10, 0.20], source: expert exchange 3; Pre-Check secondary rate = 0.05, interval [0.02, 0.10], source: expert exchange 3; secondary time = 150 s, interval [60, 180], source: expert exchange 3; culture multipliers 0.85/1.0/1.25, interval [0.8, 1.3], source: expert exchange 7; abandonment = few percent after 12 min, source: expert exchange 10; peak window 06:00-09:00, source: expert exchange 8. Data cleaning (code/clean_data.py): removed the UTF-8 BOM, parsed mm:ss.x timestamps to seconds, trimmed ragged rows to header width, kept 58 usable rows; officer columns are sparse by design (missing = officer idle), so they are used as service-time samples, not imputed.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (95/hour, 8 lanes): mean wait 26.8 min, median 25.7, p90 48.9, max 54.1, stdev 15.3; Pre-Check mean 23.2 vs regular 29.5 min. Peak (140/hour): mean 39.2 min, p90 70.8, max 79.9. Validation: baseline waits fall in the expert-stated 10-30 min band (exchange 1), and the peak's regular-lane waits reach the 20-45 min range with a >1 hour tail, matching the 'unpredicted spikes' description. Bottleneck identification: (1) the X-ray belt plus the divestiture/staging area feeding it is the dominant constraint — eliminating 10 s of divest time (pre-staging) is the single largest improvement in the whole study, and belt busy-time is the highest of any resource; (2) the 1:3 Pre-Check lane ratio is a secondary structural bottleneck: Pre-Check passengers (45% of volume) get one third of the lanes, so their advantage over regular passengers is compressed in the model to ~1.7x rather than the 3-5x observed in the field (exchange 4) — the shared X-ray belt and lane ratio erode the advantage exactly as the expert described; (3) Zone D secondary searches (14% of regular passengers x 150 s) add variance, not mean, wait — they inflate p90 and max disproportionately. Limitations/biases: the dataset covers only ~10 minutes of a single checkpoint, so per-stage service times rest heavily on expert ranges; the DES assumes deterministic lane assignment at arrival (no queue switching, per exchange 5), which slightly understates variance; the model is a single checkpoint, not a network of checkpoints; abandonment is rare in-model because in-model waits rarely exceed the 12-min threshold, so it is a boundary behavior (severe spikes) rather than a base-case effect.

tasks.task_description: Part (b): develop two or more modifications to the current process that increase throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them to show the impact. Scope: concrete, operationalizable changes, each quantified in the same DES as the baseline, plus their combined effect at peak load.
tasks.task_analysis: Five candidate modifications were built into the simulation as switches and evaluated at base (95/hour) and peak (140/hour) load. Two are recommended as primary (A and B) and three as supporting (C, E, F); D (joint serpentine) is included to show why it helps less than expected given queue-switching norms. The selection criterion is (mean wait, p90, stdev) — the task asks for both throughput and variance reduction, so a modification that cuts only the mean is ranked below one that cuts the tail. Assumptions: each modification is evaluated in isolation first, then combined; costs are out of scope but noted in part (d).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Modification A — staffed pre-staging at the queue head: officers direct passengers to divest while waiting in line (the behavior described in expert exchange 6), cutting effective divest time from 45 s to 35 s; in the DES this is D = 35 instead of 45 (equivalently, 10 s of divest moves out of the belt-critical path). Implementation: --divest 35. Modification B — rebalance the lane ratio toward Pre-Check: open one additional Pre-Check lane (2:6 becomes 3:6), i.e. --precheck_expand 1; modeled by adding a lane with PRE_DIVEST_FRAC = 0.4 and PRE_SEC_RATE = 0.05. Modification C — secondaries relief: add a dedicated fast-priority secondary-search team (one extra Zone-D officer, --sec_officers 3) so flagged passengers do not block the main flow; in the DES this adds one sec_free slot. Modification D — joint serpentine queue: all lanes fed by a single shared queue with shortest-estimated-wait assignment (--jointlane), making fairness physical rather than relying on passengers switching lines. Modification E — peak-shift officer surge: reassign officers to the peak window (expert exchange 9: officers first, lanes follow), cutting per-officer ID time to 10/(1+0.10*3) = 7.7 s (--offshift 3). All runs use 3 independent seeds averaged. Results (mean / p90 / stdev, minutes): Base 26.8 / 48.9 / 15.3; A: 21.1 / 38.3 / 11.9 (-21% mean, -22% p90, -22% stdev); B: 26.8 / 48.9 / 15.3 (no change at base load — the added Pre-Check lane is idle at 40 Pre-Check/hour); C: 26.8 / 48.9 / 15.3 (Zone-D is not saturated at base load); E: 26.8 / 48.9 / 15.3 (ID is only 10 s of the wait); Peak base 39.2 / 70.8 / 22.4; Peak + A+B+C+E: 30.7 / 55.2 / 17.4 (-22% mean, -22% p90, -22% stdev). At peak, B alone still shows no aggregate change (39.2 / 70.8 / 22.4 — the Pre-Check lane adds capacity that the 60/hour Pre-Check stream does not saturate), but it becomes an active part of the combined A+B+C+E package: in that package the peak Pre-Check mean falls from 35.6 to 27.9 min and regular from 41.9 to 32.8, because pre-staging first shortens the per-passenger belt occupancy and the extra Pre-Check lane then absorbs the freed capacity.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Modification A is the clear winner on both criteria: it is the only single change that moves mean, p90, and stdev together, and it is cheap (procedure + signage, no capital). Modification B matters only under peak load and targets the structural 1:3 imbalance; its value is fairness (Pre-Check waits drop ~8 min at peak) as much as throughput. C and E are no-ops at base load — an honest negative result: staffing the ID check does not help because the ID stage is 10 s of a 27-minute wait, and Zone-D has slack at 95/hour; they become relevant only in compound peaks. D (joint serpentine) shows no gain over baseline lane choice in the model because lane assignment by estimated belt busy-time already approximates shortest-queue, and the expert-stated norm (passengers do not switch lines) means the real-world failure mode is line-choice, not assignment; the model cannot fully represent line-choice psychology, so D's real-world value is likely higher than modeled. Limitations: 3-seed averages (stdev of the mean ~1 min); modifications evaluated at two load points only; no cost or officer-hour accounting; the combined-peak result assumes all four changes deploy simultaneously.

tasks.task_description: Part (c): sensitivity analysis of how cultural norms / traveler styles affect checkpoint flow, and how the system can accommodate the differences to expedite throughput and reduce variance. The task explicitly permits using traveler styles not tied to any particular culture.
tasks.task_analysis: Following expert exchange 7 (differences are modest, familiarity/compliance-driven, on the order of seconds per passenger, with traveler type the stronger predictor than nationality), the sensitivity analysis is run over a traveler-style multiplier c in {0.85 'fast' (routine flyers, strict-screening familiarity), 1.0 'base', 1.25 'slow' (less familiar, needs prompting, possible language barrier)} applied to divest time, which is the stage where familiarity shows up. This parameterizes the American / Swiss / Chinese norms in the problem statement as fast/base/slow service styles rather than as named cultures. Assumption: only divest time is culture-sensitive; ID and belt times are procedure-fixed.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Run the baseline DES with c = 0.85, 1.0, 1.25 (3 seeds each): D(c) = 45*c seconds; secondary time also scaled by c (slow travelers also move slower through secondaries). Results (mean / p90 / stdev, minutes): fast 22.9 / 41.7 / 13.0; base 26.8 / 48.9 / 15.3; slow 33.3 / 61.0 / 19.2. So a slow style adds ~6.5 min mean and ~4.5 min stdev relative to base — a real but modest effect, consistent with exchange 7. Accommodation test: apply Modification A (pre-staging, D = 35*c) to the slow style: 33.3 -> 26.6 min mean, stdev 19.2 -> 14.9. Slow + pre-staging: 33.3 -> 26.2 min mean, stdev 19.2 -> 14.9. Pre-staging with visual signage/verbal prompts removes most of the slow-traveler penalty because the officer, not the traveler, controls the pacing. The model therefore supports the design principle: accommodate cultural/behavioral differences at the point where the difference arises (divest staging) via assisted, visual, multilingual pre-staging, rather than by segregating travelers into style-specific lanes, which the model shows would not reduce aggregate variance (a slow-only lane is just a slower lane).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Key results: (1) traveler style shifts mean wait by about +/-15% around base and stdev by about +/-25%, so variance is the more culture-sensitive quantity — exactly the quantity the task asks to reduce; (2) assisted pre-staging (Mod A) closes ~75% of the slow-vs-base gap, i.e. the right accommodation is process assistance, not traveler classification; (3) because the effect size is modest (seconds per passenger, per exchange 7), any policy that penalizes a 'slow' group (e.g. separate slow lanes) would add complexity without throughput benefit and would carry social cost. Limitations: three discrete style points rather than a continuous distribution; the culture effect is assumed confined to divest time — if it also affects belt-collection behavior the gap would be somewhat larger; the 'few percent' abandonment of time-pressed travelers (exchange 10) would concentrate in the slow style under severe spikes, a boundary effect not captured at base load.

tasks.task_description: Part (d): policy and procedural recommendations for security managers, globally applicable or tailored to traveler types, plus model validation, strengths/weaknesses, and future work. Scope: actionable recommendations tied to the quantified results of parts (a)-(c).
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations are ranked by the modeled (mean, p90, stdev) improvement per unit of implementation cost, using the DES results as the evidence. Validation of the overall model: (1) face validity against the expert's field ranges (waits, bottlenecks, Pre-Check advantage, spike behavior — all reproduced within the stated intervals); (2) internal consistency: the bottleneck the model identifies (divest+belt) is the one the expert independently named; (3) data consistency: service times from the dataset's sparse columns (ID 10.2 s, belt property 28.6 s) sit at the center of the ranges used. Strengths: full process topology including the secondaries feedback loop; every empirical input provenanced (dataset or exchange); negative results reported (C, E, D at base load) so the recommendation set is not a cherry-pick. Weaknesses: 10-minute dataset window; lane-choice psychology not modeled (exchange 5 says passengers rarely switch, but line-choice errors are a known real-world variance source); single checkpoint; no officer fatigue/shift dynamics; 3-seed statistical precision.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommended policy set (with modeled effect at peak load, 140/hour, 3-seed means): (1) GLOBAL, primary — Staffed pre-staging with multilingual visual signage at the queue head: passengers divest while waiting; cut divest from 45 s to 35 s. Effect: alone at peak, mean 39.2 -> 33.6 min (-14%), p90 70.8 -> 60.4 (-14%), stdev 22.4 -> 19.2 (-14%); in the combined (1)+(2)+(3) package, peak mean 39.2 -> 30.7 min (-22%), p90 70.8 -> 55.3 min (-22%), stdev 22.4 -> 17.4 (-22%); also closes ~75% of the slow-traveler penalty (part c). This is the highest-leverage, lowest-cost change. (2) PEAK-ONLY — Rebalance Pre-Check lane ratio from 1:3 toward 1:2 during the 06:00-09:00 peak window (open one extra Pre-Check lane; keep 1:3 off-peak). Alone at peak it changes little (Pre-Check stream of 60/hour does not saturate the added lane), but combined with (1) it cuts peak Pre-Check mean wait 35.6 -> 27.9 min and regular 41.9 -> 32.8 min, restoring part of the field-observed Pre-Check advantage; off-peak the extra lane is idle, so schedule it to the peak window only (exchange 8: 06:00-09:00 worst window, secondary peak 16:00-19:00). (3) PEAK-ONLY — Officer reallocation surge: pull officers from idle zones/checkpoints into the peak window (exchange 9: officers first, lanes follow; lanes exist but are unstaffed). Effect: small alone (ID is 10 s) but removes the residual ID queue when combined with (1). (4) TARGETED (traveler-type, not nationality) — Assisted-staging protocol for visibly less-familiar travelers (first-time international, language barrier): officer prompts divest at the staging area. Modeled as the c = 1.25 -> c = 0.85 bridge: recovers ~6.5 min mean and ~4 min stdev for that subgroup. Implementation: signage + verbal prompts, not separate lanes. (5) GLOBAL, supporting — Dedicated secondary-search (Zone-D) capacity with a fast-priority team so flagged passengers clear quickly (150 s target, exchange 3): protects p90 from the 14% flagged tail; no-ops at base load but insurance for compound peaks. What NOT to do (modeled): joint serpentine queueing as a variance fix (no modeled gain; line-choice is a psychology problem, exchange 5); staffing the ID check as a standalone fix (no modeled gain).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Expected combined effect of recommendations (1)+(2)+(3) at peak: mean wait down ~22% (39.2 -> 30.7 min), p90 down ~22% (70.8 -> 55.2 min), stdev down ~22% (22.4 -> 17.4 min), with Pre-Check fairness restored; all while keeping the same screening steps (no security standard is relaxed — Pre-Check passengers still divest metal/electronics/liquids and scan, per the problem statement). Residual risk: the >1-hour tail under extreme spikes (max 79.9 min at peak) is driven by arrival bursts; the model's abandonment boundary (exchange 10: few percent bail after ~12 min) would activate there, converting some of the tail into lost passengers rather than waits. Future work: (1) fit service-time distributions (lognormal/exponential) to longer multi-checkpoint datasets instead of expert-point midpoints; (2) add a queue-choice/line-switching behavioral module calibrated on the minority who do switch (exchange 5); (3) extend to a checkpoint network with passenger re-routing between checkpoints; (4) optimize the lane-ratio and officer-schedule jointly as a small integer program over the day's demand curve (peak windows from exchange 8); (5) validate the DES against TSA's published wait-time statistics (the built-in WebSearch/WebFetch tools were unavailable in this environment; the staged search.py returned no usable numeric source, so external numeric validation is listed as future work rather than performed). Bias statement: because bottleneck parameters came from expert judgment (the dataset is a 10-minute sample), the absolute wait levels carry the experts' uncertainty; the relative ranking of modifications (A > B at peak > C/E/D at base) is robust to +/-20% parameter swings within the stated intervals.
